records.indication_as_stated: eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) status and lipoxygenase-mediated oxylipin biosynthesis
records.dose_quote: compared the effects of a 12-week Low-LA diet (2.5% energy) versus a High-LA diet (10.0% energy) in healthy adults
records.primary_outcome_quote: Outcomes included plasma concentrations of highly unsaturated fatty acids (HUFAs) and ex vivo zymosan-stimulated whole-blood oxylipin generation.
records.primary_result_quote: High LA exposure resulted in marked reductions in plasma n-3 eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and eicosatetraenoic acid (ETA) concentrations compared with the Low-LA arm...higher dietary LA markedly increased the ratios of ARA to EPA and ARA- to EPA-derived oxylipin species, shifting the lipid mediator balance toward a more n-6-dominant inflammatory profile.
records.direction_note: Rigorous dose-controlled RCT (NCT02962128) directly comparing Low-LA vs High-LA diets in healthy adults; high LA intake lowered EPA/ETA status and shifted oxylipin balance toward a more n-6/inflammatory profile -- a mechanistic safety-relevant signal against high LA intake.

handoff.reason: Sydney Diet Heart Study reanalysis: replacing saturated fat with LA increased all-cause/CV/CHD mortality in a secondary-prevention population.
Minnesota Coronary Experiment reanalysis: LA-for-saturated-fat replacement lowered cholesterol but showed no mortality benefit and a paradoxical mortality association.
Higher dietary LA intake associated with increased oxidation susceptibility of atherogenic lipoproteins.

identity_notes: This retrieval set was heavily contaminated with conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) records (~40 rejected as different_substance) -- CLA is a distinct structural isomer with its own identity (cla) and is not what a plain 'Linoleic Acid' label delivers; do not merge CLA efficacy/safety data into this identity. A large share of the remaining records were observational/biomarker/metabolomics studies where LA was only a measured variable, not an administered intervention (rejected not_intervention), or broad multi-exposure reviews (rejected off_topic). Among genuine LA-intervention human trials, the evidence is directionally mixed and often adversarial to a simple 'more LA is better' narrative: two landmark historical RCT reanalyses (Sydney Diet Heart Study 23386268, Minnesota Coronary Experiment 27071971) found that replacing saturated fat with LA-rich vegetable oil lowered cholesterol but increased or did not improve mortality. A recent tightly-controlled dose-response RCT (42280457, NCT02962128) found high LA intake shifts lipid mediators toward a more pro-inflammatory n-6-dominant profile and lowers EPA status. Conversely, several systematic reviews/meta-analyses (21663641, 22889633, 28752873) found no significant effect of dietary LA on tissue arachidonic acid or standard inflammatory markers -- i.e., a genuinely null/contested literature, not simply positive. Several kept RCTs (34526307, 40600308, 22959954) studied LOWERING dietary LA rather than supplementing it, which characterizes risk from high habitual intake rather than supporting supplementation. Two trials (36462055, 37550954) used RT001, a deuterated pharmaceutical-grade LA homologue, materially distinct from dietary-form LA on a supplement label. No qualifying human trial in this scope tested a simple isolated oral LA supplement against placebo for a clinical efficacy endpoint without either a confounding combination, a dose-reduction design, or a non-standard (deuterated) form.
